result:
I saved the Q3 results to `/work/answer.json`. I checked them by running the same code on Q2 first, and it reproduced all 10 of your reference values.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| a. Segment with the highest net sales | consumer, 295,880,136 |
| b. Customers with a paid order | 250 |
| c. Category with the highest net sales | sw, 310,765,700 |
| d. Month with the highest net sales | 2025-07 |
| e. Email with the largest refund total | u166@ex.com |
| f. Customers with 2 or more paid orders | 237 |
| g. Average net sales per order | 679,047 |
| h. September vs. August growth | -2.9% |

Your definitions alone didn't reproduce the Q2 values. Three extra rules were needed:
- **Time zone:** I converted order timestamps from UTC to KST (UTC+9) before deciding which day, and so which quarter and month, an order belongs to. Without this, the Q2 net sales and growth rate don't match.
- **Segment names:** the same segment is spelled several ways (`SMB` / `smb`, `Enterprise ` with a trailing space), so I trimmed spaces and lowercased them before grouping.
- **Duplicate customers:** there are 300 customer IDs but only 250 distinct emails, so I treated customers with the same email as one person. Without this, the Q2 customer counts (b, f) come out too high.

Two smaller points:
- After I checked against Q2, I also changed the refund total (e) to group by email rather than customer ID, for consistency. The Q3 answer was the same before and after, but I didn't re-run the Q2 check after that change.
- The data has no April orders at all, so the Q2 reference values only cover May and June.

STATUS: DONE
